data.title: I made a search engine worse than Elasticsearch (2024)
data.author: softwaredoug
data.article_summary: 文章讲述了作者尝试用自制的搜索库 *SearchArray* 与 *Elasticsearch* 在信息检索基准 *BEIR* 上进行性能对比，结果 *SearchArray* 在相关性（NDCG@10）和性能（查询与索引吞吐量）上均不如 *Elasticsearch*。作者深入分析了原因，指出像 *Elasticsearch* 这样的成熟搜索引擎使用了诸如 *WAND*（弱AND）等优化算法，能快速筛选出高分文档，避免不必要的计算。而 *SearchArray* 则是简单地对所有文档进行 BM25 评分并直接求和，导致性能低下。此外，*SearchArray* 使用位置索引和位图来处理短语匹配，而非传统倒排索引，这也影响了其效率。文章最终揭示了成熟搜索引擎在处理大规模数据时的优化技巧和高效性。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：对搜索功能和搜索引擎工具（如ElasticSearch等）的评价和使用体验

不同观点：
• [sh34r] 认为改进网站的搜索功能需要很长时间，且自制的搜索引擎几乎肯定不如ElasticSearch。他们强调了搜索问题的复杂性和ElasticSearch的优势。
• [intalentive] 提出在特定情况下，可以优化自制的搜索引擎，并给出了一些技术细节，如不需要通过长度或频率进行归一化处理，以及使用NLP提取关键词。
• [nchmy] 推荐Manticoresearch，认为它比ElasticSearch更容易使用且速度更快，并提到其历史和在Craigslist等网站上的应用。
• [fucalost] 支持使用Elasticsearch，认为其功能强大且生态系统健康，特别是在生产环境中，AWS的新实例类型可以显著节省成本。
• [0xB0UNCE00] 认为即使自制的搜索引擎不如Elasticsearch，但通过尝试和学习是有价值的。
• [amai] 提到了一些不如ElasticSearch的搜索引擎，并提供了相关链接以供参考。

补充讨论：
• [Alifatisk] 表示对Elasticsearch的存在感到感激。
• [niazangels] 感谢了评论提供的知识。
• [neuroelectron] 夸张地表示该讨论内容价值极高。
• [stuaxo] 表示不喜欢使用Elasticsearch，并认为在一些项目中使用ES是不必要的。

争议焦点：
• 自制搜索引擎是否值得以及是否能优于现有工具（如ElasticSearch）存在不同看法。一些评论认为特定情况下可以优化自制引擎，而多数人认为ElasticSearch已经非常强大和高效。

总结：讨论围绕搜索功能实现的难度、ElasticSearch的优劣以及其他替代工具的推荐，参与者分享了各自的技术见解和使用体验。

44194468.article_content:
I want you to share in my shame at daring to make a search library. And in this shame, you too, can experience the humility and understanding of what a real, honest-to-goodness, not side-project, search engine does to make lexical search fast.
BEIR
is a set of Information Retrieval benchmarks, oriented around question-answer use cases.
My side project,
SearchArray
adds full text search to Pandas. So naturally, to see stand in awe at my amazing developer skills, I wanted to use BEIR to compare SearchArray to Elasticsearch (w/ same query + tokenization). So I spent a Saturday integrating SearchArray into BEIR, and measuring its relevence and performance on MSMarco Passage Retrieval corpus (8M docs).
… and 🥁
Library
Elasticsearch
SearchArray
NDCG@10
0.2275
0.225
Search Throughput
90 QPS
~18 QPS
Indexing Throughput
10K Docs Per Sec
~3.5K Docs Per Sec
… Sad trombone 🎺
It’s worse in every dimension
At least
NDCG@10
is nearly right, so our BM25 calculation is correct (probably due to negligible differences in tokenization)
Imposter Syndrome anyone?
Instead of wallowing in my shame, I DO know exactly what’s going on… And it’s fairly educational. Let’s chat about why a
real
, non side-project, search engine is fast.
A Magic WAND
(Or how SearchArray is top 8m retrieval while Elasticsearch == top K retrieval)
In lexical search systems, you search for multiple terms. You take the
BM25
score of each term, and then finally, combine those into a final score for the document. IE, a search for
luke skywalker
really means:
BM25(luke) ??? BM25(skywalker)
where ??? is some mathematical operator.
In a simple “OR” query, you just take the SUM of each term for each doc, IE, a search for
luke skywalker
is
BM25(luke) + BM25(skywalker)
like so:
Term
Doc A (BM25)
Doc B (BM25)
luke
1.90
1.45
skywalker
11.51
4.3
Combined doc score  (SUM)
13.41
5.75
SearchArray just does BM25 scoring. You get back big numpy arrays of
every document
’s BM25 score. Then you combine the scores – literally using
np.sum
. Of course, that’s not what a search engine like Elasticsearch would do. Instead it has a different guarantee, it gets
the highest scoring top N
of your specified OR query.
This little bit of seemingly minute wiggle room gives search engines a great deal of latitude. Search engines can use an algorithm called
Weak-AND or WAND
to avoid work when combining multiple term scores into the final top N results.
I won’t get into the full nitty gritty of the algorithm, but here’s a key intuition to noodle over:
A scoring system like BM25 depends heavily on document frequency of a term. So rare terms - a high (1 / document frequency) - have a higher likelihood of impacting the final score, and ending up in the top K. Luckily these terms (like
skywalker
) occur on fewer documents. So we can fetch these select, elite few docs quickly in the data structure that maps
skywalker -> [... handful of matching doc ids...]
(aka postings). We can reach deeply into this list.
On the other hand, we can be much more circumspect about the boring, common term,
luke
. And that’s useful because
luke
has a very extensive postings list
luke -> [... a giant honking list of documents...]
. We’d prefer to avoid scanning all of these.
We might imagine that these lists of document ids, also is paired with its
term frequency
how often that term occurs in that document - the other major input of BM25. And if its SORTED from highest -> lowest term frequency, we can go down this list until its impossible for the BM25 score of a term to have any chance of making the top K results. Then exit early.
While WAND - and similar optimizations - helps Elasticsearch avoid work, SearchArray, gleefully does this work like an ignoramus happily giving you a giant idiotic array of BM25 scores.
When you look at this icicle graph of SearchArray’s performance doing an “OR” search, you can see all the time spent
summing
a giant array and also needlessly BM25 scoring many many documents.
SearchArray doesn’t directly store postings
Unlike most search engines, SearchArray doesn’t have postings lists of terms -> documents.
Instead, under the hood, SearchArray stores a positional index, built first-and-foremost for
phrase matching
. You give SearchArray a list of terms
['mary', 'had', 'a', 'little', 'lamb']
. It then finds every place
mary
occurs one position before
had
, etc. It does this by storing, for each terms, the positions as a
roaring bitmap
.
In our roaring bitmap, each 64 bit word has a header indicating where the positions occur (document and region in the doc). Each bit position corresponds to a position in the document. A 1 indicates this term is present, a 0 missing.
So to collect phrase matches, for
mary had
we can simply find places where one term’s bits occur adjacent to another. This can be done very fast with simple bit arithmetic.
mary
<Roaring Headers (doc id, etc)>  00000010000000    | 00000000000010
had
<Roaring Headers (doc id, etc)>  00000001000000    | 00000000000001      #< Le

data.title: How much energy does it take to think?
data.author: nsoonhui
data.article_summary: 文章探讨了大脑在思考时的能量消耗。研究显示，尽管我们在进行专注的认知任务时感觉耗费大量精力，但实际上这些任务只比休息时多消耗约5%的能量。大脑的大部分能量用于维持生理系统的平衡，而非纯粹的认知功能。进化塑造了大脑的这种能量分配模式，以保存资源。大脑仅占身体重量的2%，却消耗约20%的能量，婴儿更是高达50%。ATP（三磷酸腺苷）是大脑能量的主要来源，通过葡萄糖和氧气生成，维持神经元间的通讯和膜电位。虽然直接测量人脑ATP消耗非常侵入性，但通过PET扫描和功能磁共振成像等方法可以间接估算能量使用。文章指出，大脑不仅是思考工具，更是复杂的生物系统，受进化限制和资源管理需求的制约。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：大脑疲劳、能量消耗与思考效率之间的关系

不同观点：
• **mellow_observer** 认为现代高能量环境可能为解决大脑疲劳提供了机会，并提出如果能克服疲劳问题，将极大提高生活质量。虽然能量供应不是导致疲劳的唯一原因，但该话题受到的关注太少。
• **nameless_me** 指出，大脑需要通过休息或睡眠来排出废物，因此休息是必要的，隐含对"完全消除疲劳"可能性的质疑。
• **pmayrgundter** 提供了数据支持，指出大脑的能量消耗仅比基础代谢率略高，思考所消耗的能量相对较小，暗示思考并不是大脑能量消耗的主要因素。
• **teleforce** 强调大脑占身体质量的2%却消耗20-25%的能量，指出讨论中忽视了线粒体的重要性，认为这是理解能量消耗的关键。
• **gleenn** 通过个人经历说明高强度思考确实会导致更快的能量消耗，即使是在无糖饮料情况下，身体依然渴望糖分补充能量。
• **jonplackett** 提出在高压下感受到的时间膨胀是否与神经元最大化发射频率有关，暗示大脑在极限情况下的运作机制可能与日常状态不同。
• **Perz1val** 半开玩笑地询问是否可以通过药物将神经元发射频率从4Hz提升到100Hz，认为即使增加能量消耗，也能通过食物补充。
• **chvid** 质疑“思考”的定义，认为社会互动等复杂任务对大脑的负荷远高于简单任务，因此思考的能量消耗不能一概而论。
• **fside** 提出大脑是高效的能量节约者，认为超级计算机或AI的设计应更多关注效率而非纯粹的处理能力，类似于大脑的运作方式。
• **debuggerson** 询问不思考时的能量消耗是否与高强度思考不同，认为不同类型的思考可能对应不同的能量消耗模式。
• **xyzzy123** 观察到儿童在集中精力时会呼吸加重，对这一现象表示好奇，但未提供解释。
• **krzat** 认为大型语言模型（LLM）仅模拟了大脑功能的一小部分，暗示人工推理可能比人工大脑更容易实现。
• **flurdy** 提到国际象棋大师在长时间思考时消耗大量能量，尽管这是一项静坐的活动，暗示高强度的思维活动确实会导致显著的能量消耗。

补充讨论：
- 讨论中多次提到能量消耗的具体数据和生理机制，如线粒体和神经元发射频率，显示出对大脑能量消耗细节的关注。
- 争议焦点在于是否有可能通过外部手段克服大脑疲劳以及思考对大脑能量消耗的真实影响。一些观点认为高强度思考确实消耗更多能量，而另一些观点则强调大脑的基础代谢已经占据了大部分能量消耗。
- 对思考的定义和不同类型的思考对能量消耗的影响也有不同看法，尤其是社会互动与单纯任务之间的对比。

How Much Energy Does It Take To Think?
By
Conor Feehly
June 4, 2025
Studies of neural metabolism reveal our brain’s effort to keep us alive and the evolutionary constraints that sculpted our most complex organ.

You’ve just gotten home from an exhausting day. All you want to do is put your feet up and zone out to whatever is on television. Though the inactivity may feel like a well-earned rest, your brain is not just chilling. In fact, it is using nearly as much energy as it did during your stressful activity, according to recent research.
Sharna Jamadar
, a neuroscientist at Monash University in Australia, and her colleagues reviewed research from her lab and others around the world to estimate the
metabolic cost of cognition
— that is, how much energy it takes to power the human brain. Surprisingly, they concluded that effortful, goal-directed tasks use only 5% more energy than restful brain activity. In other words, we use our brain just a small fraction more when engaging in focused cognition than when the engine is idling.
It often feels as though we allocate our mental energy through strenuous attention and focus. But the new research builds on a growing understanding that the majority of the brain’s function goes to maintenance. While many neuroscientists have historically focused on active, outward cognition, such as attention, problem-solving, working memory and decision-making, it’s becoming clear that beneath the surface, our background processing is a hidden hive of activity. Our brains regulate our bodies’ key physiological systems, allocating resources where they’re needed as we consciously and subconsciously react to the demands of our ever-changing environments.
“There is this sentiment that the brain is for thinking,” said
Jordan Theriault
, a neuroscientist at Northeastern University who was not involved in the new analysis. “Where, metabolically, [the brain’s function is] mostly spent on managing your body, regulating and coordinating between organs, managing this expensive system which it’s attached to, and navigating a complicated external environment.”

The neuroscientist Sharna Jamadar compiled data from simultaneous MRI and PET imaging to estimate the brain’s energy use.
Emma Liang
The brain is not purely a cognition machine, but an object sculpted by evolution — and therefore constrained by the tight energy budget of a biological system. Thinking may make you feel tired, then, not because you are out of energy, but because you have evolved to preserve resources. This study of neural metabolism, when tied to research on the dynamics of the brain’s electrical firing, points to the competing evolutionary forces that explain the limitations, scope and efficiencies of our cognitive capabilities.
The Cost of a Predictive Engine
The human brain is incredibly expensive to run. At roughly 2% of body weight, the organ gorges on 20% of our body’s energetic resources. “It’s hugely metabolically demanding,” Jamadar said. For infants, that number is closer to 50%.
The brain is not purely a cognition machine, but an object sculpted by evolution.
The brain’s energy comes in the form of the molecule adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which cells make from glucose and oxygen. A tremendous expanse of thin capillaries — an estimated 400 miles of vascular wiring — weaves through brain tissue to carry glucose- and oxygen-rich blood to neurons and other brain cells. Once synthesized within cells, ATP powers communication between neurons, which enact the brain’s functions. Neurons carry electrical signals to their synapses, which allow the cells to exchange molecular messages; the strength of a signal determines whether they will release molecules (or “fire”). If they do, that molecular signal determines whether the next neuron will pass on the message, and so on. Maintaining what are known as membrane potentials — stable voltages across a neuron’s membrane that ensure that the cell is primed to fire when called upon — is known to account for at least half of the brain’s total energy budget.
Measuring ATP directly in the human brain is highly invasive. So, for their paper, Jamadar’s lab

data.article_summary: Dreamstar是一家由Joshua Dominic和Thomas Eastmond创立的私人铁路创业公司，计划重现1940年代洛杉矶和旧金山之间豪华过夜列车的魅力。该公司设想提供中等距离的高端卧铺列车服务，包括全卧室设施、车上美食和五星级酒店服务。Dreamstar计划使用Southern Pacific的Lark路线，并与Union Pacific签署了轨道使用协议。列车将尽量减少停靠站点，以确保乘客的连续休息，同时减少碳排放。车厢将包括四种不同级别的私人舱室，并提供餐饮、休息室和水疗等设施。虽然具体定价尚未确定，但公司目标是与航班加酒店、Amtrak类似服务的费用竞争。Dreamstar计划在2028年洛杉矶奥运会前开始运营，目前正与多家供应商和监管机构合作推进项目。

44199005.article_content:
Can a passenger rail startup bring back the glamour of luxury overnight trains connecting Los Angeles and San Francisco that haven’t been seen since the 1940s?
Co-founders Joshua Dominic and Thomas Eastmond think so — and there’s a connection to freight rail at the heart of their proposal.
Dreamstar is a private venture reimagining medium-length passenger service in a setting that harks back to the heyday of first-class trains with all-bedroom accommodations, onboard gourmet dining and five-star hotel hospitality.
“Dreamstar started from a deeply personal frustration with the state of American travel,” said Dominic, in an interview. “After experiencing modern rail across Europe and Asia in my 20s, I kept asking, ‘Why don’t we have this in the U.S.?’ Years later, after hundreds of business and leisure trips that forced a choice between wasting precious daytime or sacrificing sleep, the idea crystallized: Build a better alternative. Dreamstar is our answer — a rail service that brings rest, reliability and elegance to medium-distance travel.”
The Southern Pacific’s Lark was the last domestic all-sleeper train to run exclusively in one state, operating two daily trains between San Francisco and LA. Espee added coaches after the Second World War; Amtrak’s all-sleeper California Zephyr ended service between Chicago and Emeryville, California, in 1997.
Dreamstar plans to run over much of the Lark’s route, having signed a memorandum of agreement for track access with Union Pacific, which merged with SP in 1996. That includes 400 miles between San Jose and Ventura, which the partners say has minimal overnight freight and passenger traffic.
Southbound Southern Pacific No. 76, the Lark, on Santa Susana Pass near Chatsworth, Calif., on Oct. 14, 1950. (Photo: William D. Middleton)
Union Pacific (NYSE:
UNP
) in a statement confirmed that it is in formal negotiations with Dreamstar but offered no details.
Freight tracks are an essential component of the original proposal, like another recent passenger train startup, Brightline, which started out running on the tracks of sister company Florida East Coast Railway.
Dominic said Dreamstar is working on access agreements with commuter agencies Caltrain and Metrolink, as well as the agency that manages Los Angeles Union Passenger Terminal.
“The flagship route is designed as an overnight, limited-stop service optimized for uninterrupted rest,” said Dominic. “We aim to keep stops to a minimum while ensuring operational viability and regional access.”
The startup also claims its trains will reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 75% compared to flying.
While pricing specifics are still being. worked on, Dominic said Dreamstar would be competitive with a flight-plus-hotel, last minute flight/business class flight, flying a family of four, and what Amtrak is currently charging for similar accommodations. Tickets will be sold online, similar to hotel and flight bookings.
Conceptual renderings emulate the proportions and outlines of contemporary passenger equipment. The cars follow the profile of the original Budd Hi-Level cars of Santa Fe’s El Capitan,
an all-coach train running between Los Angeles and Chicago, that were passed on to Amtrak and eventually replaced by the bilevel Superliners, also manufactured by Budd, which included sleeping accommodations.
There are four classes of accommodations — called private cabins — including standard, bedroom, stateroom and family room sleeping six, as well as lounges, dining spaces and a spa.
Rendering of Dreamstar stateroom. (Photo: Dreamstar)
The renderings also depict Dreamstar’s Auto Ferry, car transporters similar to those of Amtrak’s Auto Train.
Dreamstar’s original proposal in 2018 called for construction of an all-new train. Now, the company plans to rebuild four previously owned cars.
“We’ve completed the concept development phase in partnership with BMW Designworks,” Dominic said. “The next step is further refinement and engineering drawings. We’ve identified a handful of potential suppliers and are evaluating next steps.”
The Los Angeles design studio has worked with aircraft maker Embraer, John Deere and Singapore Airlines, among many other clients.
Construction of rolling stock is expected to take 18 to 24 months, with service to begin prior to the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
A locomotive supplier has yet to be selected, “but we’ve identified several viable options that align with our performance and emissions goals. We’ve reviewed a few promising options and are continuing to explore the right partners for both operations and maintenance.”
The company said location planning is underway for maintenance facilities in parallel with operational modeling.
Dominic said Dreamstar is working with industry experts to smooth the way through regulatory approval processes.
At the same time, California homebuilder Bill Lyon has dropped $100,000 on Dreamstar.

data.title: An Interactive Guide to Rate Limiting
data.author: sagyam
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：数据存储和速率限制算法的选择，尤其是在水平扩展服务和API请求管理的场景下。

不同观点：
• joshstrange：询问用户/组织的请求跟踪的最佳数据存储方案，提到了几种选择，如Redis/Valkey、Postgres、DynamoDB。
• hxtk：提出为何很少见到基于服务请求成本或动态学习系统容量的速率限制算法。提到路由器缓冲管理中的算法（如Stochastic Fair Blue），但指出难以应用于HTTP请求场景，因为需要定义每个请求的成功/失败指标。还提到Google的Zanzibar系统中简要提及了基于CPU时间分配的速率限制，但没有详细说明。
• conradludgate：推荐通用信元率算法（GCRA），认为其实现简单，无需后台任务和最小状态存储。GCRA不仅可作为速率限制器，还能作为节流实现，并能自然转换为漏桶算法。
• jsw：认为AIMD算法（加性增加，乘性减少）与令牌桶结合，可以很好地适应后端容量，优于断路器。
• fside：好奇是否有人在遇到实际扩展问题后切换算法，并询问是否有只在规模化时才显现的“坑”。

补充讨论：
• behnamoh：批评某些博客的用户体验，如看到要求使用Google登录的提示就关闭页面。
• chrisweekly：提到《HPBN》（High-Performance Browser Networking）一书，认为其包含相关概念。
• tonyhart7 和 phelm：推荐了另一篇关于速率限制算法的文章链接。
• tra3：提到尝试解释断路器和自适应并发以改善分布式单体性能的困难，认为可视化工具很有帮助。
• mcdow：对交互部分的构建工具表示兴趣。
• onionbagle：好奇是否有人实现了这些算法，并询问使用的技术。
• buggeryorkshire：提到CGNAT在之前工作中引发的问题，但未被提及。

争议焦点：
• mtlyncr：批评文章像是由AI生成且未经仔细审查，指出文章结构和样式问题，如反复使用“Working:”作为标题，以及在暗模式下示例不可用的问题。

这些讨论展示了在数据存储选择和速率限制算法上的多样观点和实际应用中的挑战，尤其是规模化时的潜在问题。

data.title: Odyc.js – A tiny JavaScript library for narrative games
data.author: achtaitaipai
data.article_summary: Odyc.js 是一个小型 JavaScript 库，旨在帮助用户创建视频游戏，即使没有编程经验也能轻松上手。它提供了简单易用的工具，让初学者可以通过编码学习游戏开发。用户可以利用该库制作自己的游戏，同时还能浏览和借鉴他人作品的展示库以获取灵感。Odyc.js 专注于让游戏开发变得更易于访问和有趣，是学习编程和游戏设计的理想选择。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：对一个JavaScript游戏库的评价与讨论

不同观点：
• [socalgal2] 对标题中的"narrative games"（叙事游戏）提出质疑，认为库的主页并没有明确说明这是针对叙事游戏的，且对什么是叙事游戏表示困惑。她指出，通过谷歌搜索"narrative game"的结果与她看到的示例游戏不符，并质疑该库在制作叙事游戏方面是否有其他游戏引擎不具备的独特功能。

• [kevinsync] 分享了一个具体的游戏链接（Magic Mushroom），并对该游戏表示赞赏，但没有对库本身的功能或定义做进一步讨论。

• [c0nfused] 对该库的整体设计表示赞赏，提到自己曾写过多个JavaScript游戏引擎，而这个库在快速制作游戏和深度研究之间找到了一个很好的平衡点。他计划用这个库来快速制作小游戏以娱乐孩子。

• [NotAnOtter] 认为该库是一个很好的学习工具，特别适合10岁左右的孩子，比Scratch等工具更适合，因为Scratch被设计得过于低龄化。他还建议可以为此工具开设儿童课程，并认为可以在游戏资产的程序生成方面做进一步开发。

• [halfmatthalfcat] 简单表达了对该库的赞赏，但没有进一步展开。

• [fudged71] 分享了一段代码示例，展示了如何使用该库进行简单的游戏对话，但没有对库本身的功能做评价。

• [matkurianski] 对项目表示赞赏，但指出项目是开源的却没有明确的许可证。他询问是否可以添加许可证，以便开发者能够了解可以如何修改和发布他们的分支，并具体询问是否可以将项目翻译成其他语言。

• [hahahacorn] 认为该库非常酷，并分享了一个个人故事，讲述自己在发现这个库之前正好在制作一个叙事 romance 游戏，且从未开发过任何游戏。他认为这个库正好解决了他的需求，并认为这个巧合非常惊人。

• [sciolizer] 提到该库让他想起了PuzzleScript，并提供了一个链接，但没有对库本身的功能做进一步评价。

• [navs] 对库中的canvas视频录制功能表示好奇，表示希望实现类似的功能，但没有对库的其他方面做评价。

• [eldog_] 赞赏了编辑器中的类型使用，特别是它能够识别模板精灵的引用，并在调用函数时传递错误参数的情况下高亮错误。

• [ryoshu] 表示非常喜欢这个库，认为它正好符合一个副项目的要求，但没有进一步展开。

• [wdiamond] 认为这是一个很棒的产品，类似于Scratch，但没有进一步展开。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点在于什么是“叙事游戏”以及该库是否特别适合制作此类游戏。
• 一些用户对该库的教育用途表示赞赏，特别是对于儿童学习编程的潜力。
• 部分用户对库的具体功能（如代码高亮、视频录制）表示赞赏，并分享了使用场景和个人经验。
• 开源许可证问题也被提出，用户关心是否可以对项目进行修改和发布。

data.title: Weaponizing Dependabot: Pwn Request at its finest
data.author: chha
data.article_summary: 本文介绍了如何通过“Confused Deputy”攻击利用GitHub的Dependabot自动合并恶意代码。Dependabot通常用于自动更新项目依赖，但若配置不当，可能被攻击者利用。攻击者可以通过以下步骤进行攻击：首先， fork目标仓库；然后，在fork中添加恶意代码并启用Dependabot，使其生成包含恶意代码的更新分支；接着，创建指向原仓库的Pull Request，触发自动合并工作流。由于`github.actor`不总是指代PR创建者，攻击者可利用此特性触发自动合并，绕过保护规则，最终将恶意代码合并入原仓库。文章还披露了两种新的攻击技术，以扩展已有方法。

44199597.article_content:
Blog Articles
Weaponizing Dependabot: Pwn Request at its finest
Sébastien Graveline
TL;DR
: Your trusty Dependabot (and other GitHub bots) might be an unwitting accomplice. Through "Confused Deputy" attacks, they can be tricked into merging malicious code. This doesn’t stop here. It can escalate to full command injection via crafted branch names and even bypass branch protection rules. Plus, we disclose two new TTPs to build upon previously known techniques.
Introduction
Ah,
Dependabot
!
GitHub's built-in butler, tirelessly checks if your dependencies are fresh and, if not, prepares a PR with the updates. What a lifesaver, right? But, as with any cog in an automated system, there’s always the potential for rust. In this story, it is the
deputy confusion
attack.
Meet Dependabot: Your Automated Dependency Butler
So, how does this magic work? You can boss Dependabot around using a
.github/dependabot.yml
file (check out the
Dependabot options reference
).
Once active, Dependabot periodically scans your repo, guided by its config file. It also perks up and re-scans whenever you tweak this file or poke it via the
https://github.com/<Owner>/<Repo>/network/updates
tab.
When Dependabot spots an outdated dependency, it kicks off a workflow (you'll see "Dependabot Updates" pop up in your Actions tab). Then, it creates a new branch, usually named something like
dependabot/<module_type>/<registry>/<package_name>/<new_version>
. Finally, it opens a Pull Request to your default branch with all the suggested changes.
The "Confused Deputy" Problem: Wait, Who Asked You To Do That?
Now, let's talk about the
Confused Deputy Problem
. It's a classic vulnerability class (
CWE-441
, if you're into that sort of thing) where a trusted party (our "deputy") is tricked by an attacker into performing an action. The deputy thinks it’s doing honest work, but it's carrying out the attacker's nefarious plan.
Some workflows are sensitive – they might have special permissions or access to secrets, so many developers added a user check at the beginning of them. Just to make sure it was triggered by a trusted user.
Naturally, folks got a bit tired of manually approving every single Dependabot PR. "It's just a version update," they'd say. Others might say: "and we usually just end up blindly merging it anyway!". So, they created workflows to auto-merge PRs if the creator was Dependabot.
Something like this GitHub Actions workflow:
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
auto-merge:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
if: ${
{
github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]'
}}
steps:
- run:
gh pr merge
$ -d -m
Seems safe, doesn't it? After all, Dependabot is trusted, and an attacker can't just force it to open a PR on a repo they don't control… Here's the trick:
github.actor
does not always refer to the actual creator of the Pull Request. It's the user who caused the latest event that triggered the workflow.
So, if an attacker could somehow force Dependabot into making a change that triggers this auto-merge workflow, they can merge their own malicious code.
Now, an attacker can't directly command Dependabot on a repo they don't have rights to. So, what can they make Dependabot do? Let's look at the events Dependabot is able to trigger:
Event
Action
From fork
Command
pull_request_target
,
pull_request
When creating or updating a pull request.
true
@dependabot recreate
issue_comment
When showing information.
false
@dependabot show <dependency name> ignore conditions
push
When pushing to the branch, when merging etc.
false
@dependabot merge
create
When creating a new branch.
false
N/A
delete
When deleting a branch.
false
@dependabot close
workflow_run
It simply gets triggered as a side-effect of another (named) workflow running or completing.
true
Relevant if the parent workflow was triggered using one of the above commands.
The juicy one here is that Dependabot can be forced to update a Pull Request, even one originating from a fork!
Here's the evil plan:
Fork It
: Attacker forks a target repository. This repo has one of those "auto-merge if Dependabot" workflows.
Rig it
: Attacker adds their
malicious payload
to the
Default branch
of their fork.
Wake Up, Dependabot!
: Attacker enables Dependabot on their fork and adds an obviously outdated dependency to get its attention (often at the time you fork, this pre-requisite will already be met).
Dependabot Does Its Thing
: Dependabot creates its update branch on the fork. Since this branch is based on the fork's own Default branch, the now includes the attacker's payload (
through the refs/pulls/ read-only namespace
).
The Bait
: Attacker creates a Pull Request from this weaponized Dependabot branch on their fork, targeting the original (victim) repository.
Firing blanks
: This new PR triggers the auto-merge workflow in the victim repo. However, at this point,
github.actor
is the attacker, so the if condition fails, and the workflow doesn't merge anything.
Confused, are you?
: Attacker goes back to the original Pull Request in their fork

data.title: Small Programs and Languages
data.author: todsacerdoti
data.article_summary:
文章讨论了小型Forth实现以及小型程序的吸引力。小型程序更易于阅读和理解，例如一个有趣的功能若仅用20行代码实现，会比用2000行实现更引人关注。文章列举了几个例子，如Luke Jackson的25行JavaScript库`ijk`，以及Philippe Brochard的46字节Forth实现。作者还提到Roger K.W. Hui描述的单页C语言解释器，以及William Byrd演讲中提到的精美Lisp解释器。

文章进一步探讨了这些小型程序的意义，指出它们不仅是一种编程娱乐，还揭示了程序的最小复杂性。例如，名片大小的光线追踪器展示了光线追踪器的最低复杂度。作者还提到了Kolmogorov复杂性，即生成某个对象的最短程序长度，并指出小型实现帮助人们理解编程语言的基本概念。最后，提到Justine Tunney实现的436字节LISP，展示了垃圾回收语言的核心可以压缩到如此小的规模。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：小型编程语言与Kolmogorov复杂性的关系，小型语言的表达能力与实用性，以及具体的小型语言实现和其设计哲学。

不同观点：
• **tromp**：Kolmogorov复杂性激发了对最小且最具表达力语言的探索，并定义了不同 flavor 的 Kolmogorov 复杂性。tromp 强调通过小型语言来理解程序的最小尺寸和复杂性。
• **karmakaze**：小型语言通常是创建特定编程抽象的原型语言，像 Lisp 这样的语言由于每个项目自成一个方言而不易普及。相比之下，像 Clojure 这样更具意见性且功能齐全的语言更实用。
• **antilisp**：实现小型语言是一种极好的学习体验，通过实现语言可以发现新的创新机会。例如，在 Lisp 中将宏和公理作为函数类型的特例处理，并通过解释器决定运行时的评估方式。
• **nicolaskruchten**：通过量化和可视化库来研究小型语言的小型性与表达能力的权衡，得出了一些有趣的结论。
• **bradain**：不喜欢小型 Lisp 实现，认为真正的 Lisp 应该是元循环的，即解释器能够解释自身。使用简化技巧虽然缩短了代码，但失去了元循环评估的能力。
• **norir**：Kolmogorov 复杂性虽然有趣但具有误导性，因为解释某些极小程序时需要依赖外部上下文和公理，而这些无法在程序本身中定义。

补充讨论：
• **forinti**：20世纪80年代的计算机杂志经常刊登小型项目，这些项目既能教学又足够小，可以手动输入学习。
• **asplake**：寻找类似于ML或更具Lisp风格但支持柯里化的微小语言，可能是为了学习和趣味。
• **dunham**：Meta II 是一个用于编写编译器的小型语言，包括自编译能力，具有历史和技术意义。
• **xelxebar**：提到一个仅有41行的极其简洁的C语言Lisp解释器，强调了可读代码的重要性。
• **muth02446**：Cwerg 是一种类似C的低级语言，具有Python风格的语法，前端代码限制在10k行以内，展示了小型语言的另一种实现方式。
• **agentultra**：小型编码和尺寸编码是有趣的活动，参考demo场景。正在开发最小的事件存储数据库，作为企业软件开发之外的调剂。
• **anthk**：提到一个网站（https://t3x.org）提供多种小型语言，如Lisp、Forth和Pascal等，并指出TCL（jimtcl）具有强大的CLI/TUI工具开发能力。
• **codr7**：最近在多个宿主语言中开发小型语言的基板/引导程序，展示了小型语言的实现和探索的持续性。

争议焦点：
• **小型语言的实用性**：karmakaze 认为小型语言如 Lisp 因为自定义方言的问题不易普及，而 antilisp 和 tromp 则强调小型语言的实现和研究价值。
• **Kolmogorov 复杂性的实际应用**：norir 认为 Kolmogorov 复杂性在实际应用中具有误导性，因为外部上下文和公理的依赖性，而 tromp 则认为这是理解程序最小尺寸和复杂性的关键。

总体而言，讨论围绕小型语言的设计、实现、实用性以及其在Kolmogorov复杂性研究中的应用展开，展示了不同开发者和研究者的视角和经验。

44200797.article_content:
My
Implementing a Forth
article got some
great feedback, particularly around the subject of tiny Forth implementations.
(And it was an excuse to list some of the tiniest Forths I’ve seen.)
I know I’m not alone in seeing the appeal of tiny Forths, tiny languages, tiny
programs, and just small stuff in general. What’s up with that, anyway?
The appeal of tiny programs
Tiny programs are approachable.
If I see that something is 200 lines of code, I’m
much
more likely to
read it than if it’s 2,000 or 20,000 lines.
What’s more, if it’s a program that does something interesting in 20 lines when
I was
expecting
2,000, then I’m going to be very, very interested to read
those 20 lines!
When I was researching DOM diffing libraries
prior to creating
RetroV
, one of
the repos I looked at was
ijk
by Luke Jackson.
I was pretty used to looking at fat JavaScript
libraries at that point, so when I cracked open
the source file for ijk, I was really surprised.
Here’s the source:
index.js
(githubusercontent.com).
Just 25 lines!
I was instantly intrigued.
More recently, one of the responses to my aforementioned Forth article was
Philippe Brochard with a 46 byte "Forth".
46 bytes!
It’s
so
small, I can just put the hexdump right here:
50b8 8e00 31d8 e8ff 0017 003c 0575 00ea
5000 3c00 7401 eb02 e8ee 0005 0588 eb47
b8e6 0200 d231 14cd e480 7580 c3f4
(See my update to
Implementing a Forth
for more
about this artifact.)
Sure, very few people jump at a chance to read raw machine code. But that’s
exactly my point.  Something
this
small doesn’t feel so scary, right? I mean,
46 bytes. If you put the effort into it, you
know
you can figure out how it
works eventually.
This next one almost serves as a counter-example because the code is so dense
and frightening, but I can’t help mentioning it anyway.
One of my favorite software stories is Roger K.W. Hui’s Appendix A "Incunabulum"
from
An Implementation of J
in which he describes Arthur Whitney writing
an array-based language interpreter,
"…​on
one page
and in one afternoon â an interpreter fragment
on the AT&T 3B1 computer. I studied this interpreter for about a week for its
organization and programming style…​"
Hui can list the entire interpreter in the appendix because it’s just that
single page,
122 lines
of incredibly cryptic C, which you can view here:
https://code.jsoftware.com/wiki/Essays/Incunabulum
I haven’t personally tackled that puzzle yet, but it’s in my unwritten list of
dense computer things that I would print out and take with me if I suddenly
found myself cast out of society and forced to go live alone up on a mountain
or something.
(By the way, J is in the family of array languages which include APL.
If you enjoy brevity, cryptic programming puzzles, and high performance
numerical computing, these languages have got you covered!)
Something else that would certainly need to be in the collection I take to that
lonely mountain would have to be
The Most Beautiful Program Ever Written
,
according to the title of a talk by William Byrd.  Spoiler alert: It’s this
Lisp interpreter in Lisp:
(define eval-expr
(lambda (expr env)
(pmatch expr
[`,x (guard (symbol? x))
(env x)]
[`(lambda (,x) ,body)
(lambda (arg)
(eval-expr body (lambda (y)
(if (eq? x y)
arg
(env y)))))]
[`(,rator ,rand)
((eval-expr rator env)
(eval-expr rand env))])))
(The above is from Alberto Zaccagni’s
transcription of the code
(github.com) shown in Byrd’s slide.)
Recreation or fundamental truths?
Now, we all know that
code golfing
(wikipedia.org) is
a programmer’s recreational game, and just for fun, right?
But is any of this actually useful?
Actually, I’ll go one step further and say that these examples are
more than just useful. They are

44200797.article_summary:
文章讨论了小型Forth实现以及小型程序的吸引力。小型程序更易于阅读和理解，例如一个有趣的功能若仅用20行代码实现，会比用2000行实现更引人关注。文章列举了几个例子，如Luke Jackson的25行JavaScript库`ijk`，以及Philippe Brochard的46字节Forth实现。作者还提到Roger K.W. Hui描述的单页C语言解释器，以及William Byrd演讲中提到的精美Lisp解释器。

文章进一步探讨了这些小型程序的意义，指出它们不仅是一种编程娱乐，还揭示了程序的最小复杂性。例如，名片大小的光线追踪器展示了光线追踪器的最低复杂度。作者还提到了Kolmogorov复杂性，即生成某个对象的最短程序长度，并指出小型实现帮助人们理解编程语言的基本概念。最后，提到Justine Tunney实现的436字节LISP，展示了垃圾回收语言的核心可以压缩到如此小的规模。
44200797.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：小型编程语言与Kolmogorov复杂性的关系，小型语言的表达能力与实用性，以及具体的小型语言实现和其设计哲学。

不同观点：
• **tromp**：Kolmogorov复杂性激发了对最小且最具表达力语言的探索，并定义了不同 flavor 的 Kolmogorov 复杂性。tromp 强调通过小型语言来理解程序的最小尺寸和复杂性。
• **karmakaze**：小型语言通常是创建特定编程抽象的原型语言，像 Lisp 这样的语言由于每个项目自成一个方言而不易普及。相比之下，像 Clojure 这样更具意见性且功能齐全的语言更实用。
• **antilisp**：实现小型语言是一种极好的学习体验，通过实现语言可以发现新的创新机会。例如，在 Lisp 中将宏和公理作为函数类型的特例处理，并通过解释器决定运行时的评估方式。
• **nicolaskruchten**：通过量化和可视化库来研究小型语言的小型性与表达能力的权衡，得出了一些有趣的结论。
• **bradain**：不喜欢小型 Lisp 实现，认为真正的 Lisp 应该是元循环的，即解释器能够解释自身。使用简化技巧虽然缩短了代码，但失去了元循环评估的能力。
• **norir**：Kolmogorov 复杂性虽然有趣但具有误导性，因为解释某些极小程序时需要依赖外部上下文和公理，而这些无法在程序本身中定义。

补充讨论：
• **forinti**：20世纪80年代的计算机杂志经常刊登小型项目，这些项目既能教学又足够小，可以手动输入学习。
• **asplake**：寻找类似于ML或更具Lisp风格但支持柯里化的微小语言，可能是为了学习和趣味。
• **dunham**：Meta II 是一个用于编写编译器的小型语言，包括自编译能力，具有历史和技术意义。
• **xelxebar**：提到一个仅有41行的极其简洁的C语言Lisp解释器，强调了可读代码的重要性。
• **muth02446**：Cwerg 是一种类似C的低级语言，具有Python风格的语法，前端代码限制在10k行以内，展示了小型语言的另一种实现方式。
• **agentultra**：小型编码和尺寸编码是有趣的活动，参考demo场景。正在开发最小的事件存储数据库，作为企业软件开发之外的调剂。
• **anthk**：提到一个网站（https://t3x.org）提供多种小型语言，如Lisp、Forth和Pascal等，并指出TCL（jimtcl）具有强大的CLI/TUI工具开发能力。
• **codr7**：最近在多个宿主语言中开发小型语言的基板/引导程序，展示了小型语言的实现和探索的持续性。

争议焦点：
• **小型语言的实用性**：karmakaze 认为小型语言如 Lisp 因为自定义方言的问题不易普及，而 antilisp 和 tromp 则强调小型语言的实现和研究价值。
• **Kolmogorov 复杂性的实际应用**：norir 认为 Kolmogorov 复杂性在实际应用中具有误导性，因为外部上下文和公理的依赖性，而 tromp 则认为这是理解程序最小尺寸和复杂性的关键。

总体而言，讨论围绕小型语言的设计、实现、实用性以及其在Kolmogorov复杂性研究中的应用展开，展示了不同开发者和研究者的视角和经验。

data.title: The Coleco Adam Computer
data.author: rbanffy
data.article_summary: The Coleco Adam电脑是玩具和游戏机制造商Coleco于1983年推出的一款家用电脑，旨在与Commodore 64竞争，但最终未能实现预期，于1985年停产。Coleco曾是知名的玩具制造商，1982年成功推出ColecoVision游戏机，采用Z-80 CPU及德州仪器的图形和声音芯片，性能接近任天堂NES。Coleco Adam最初定价525美元，包含80K RAM、全行程键盘、磁带存储、打印机及软件，计划通过与现有ColecoVision游戏机结合来吸引消费者。然而，Coleco低估了生产难度，价格升至725美元，且延迟发布，缺陷率高，存储设备和打印机存在设计问题。与此同时，Commodore解决了生产问题，售出300万台C64，而Coleco因供货不足和产品缺陷错失机会，最终失败。

44199437.article_content:
Dave Farquhar
Retro Computing
June 5, 2025
April 5, 2025
1 Comment
The Coleco Adam computer was a 1983 attempt by toy and game console maker Coleco to enter the growing home computer market. Critics and consumers looked forward to the computer after Coleco unveiled it June 5, 1983, but it never lived up to that anticipation. Coleco discontinued the Adam in 1985. Nevertheless, the Adam remains an interesting might-have-been.
Who was Coleco?
The Coleco Adam computer was supposed to give the Commodore 64 a run for its money but failed to live up to its enormous promise. It was one of the biggest computer flops of the 1980s.
Coleco was a leading maker of toys, particularly electronic toys. In the 1970s, it competed with Atari, releasing Pong-like consoles as part of its Telstar product line.
In 1982, it introduced its very successful
Coleco Vision game console
, which teamed a Z-80 CPU with sound and graphics chips from Texas Instruments. With a computer-grade CPU, graphics and sound chips, the Coleco Vision provided advanced capabilities for its day, much closer to those of the
Nintendo NES
than the
Atari 2600
. Coleco also sold an
Atari 2600 clone
.
Enter the Coleco Adam computer
In 1983, the home computer industry was far from decided. Commodore led the industry in sales, but looked vulnerable. Its
VIC-20
computer was underpowered and sales were fading fast. The
Commodore 64
was selling well, but Commodore was having trouble keeping up with demand, especially for peripherals like disk drives. The Commodore 64 was a bargain at $299 compared to more expensive computers from
Apple
and Atari, but a bare $299 computer wasn’t very useful. You really needed a disk drive and a printer to do anything with the system.
Coleco saw an opening. In January 1983, Coleco announced the Coleco Adam computer. For $525, Coleco promised a complete system. It would have 80K of RAM, a full-travel keyboard, tape-based storage, a daisywheel printer, and software including the game
Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom
and a word processor. It could use an inexpensive television for a monitor, like other home computers of the day. The Adam was a lot like the
Texas Instruments TI-99/4A
, but by using a Zilog CPU, it was easier to program. It looked like what the TI-99/4A should have been.
The Adam gave protection to the Coleco Vision game console as well. Commodore successfully attacked Atari by saying it made more sense to buy one of their computers rather than a machine that could only play video games. Coleco introduced a version of the Adam that plugged into an existing Coleco Vision console, turning it into a full-blown computer system. This wasn’t a new idea. Rival APF had tried this in 1978-79 with its
MP1000 console
and
Imagination Machine add-on
. But the time seemed right in 1983 to try the idea again.
It looked like a winner. It was a real computer. The industry knew how to develop for it since it used well-known and well-understood chips. It could play existing Coleco Vision games, so there was stuff you could do with it on day 1. The kids could do their homework on it with the included word processor, and they could play Coleco Vision games on it.
Why the Coleco Adam computer failed
Coleco would have been difficult to compete with if it had delivered. But Coleco underestimated what it would take to bring the Adam to market. Coleco had to raise the price to $599 and then to $725. Then it failed to meet the release date of September 1. It kept pushing the release date out two weeks and finally managed to release the computer in late October in limited quantities.
Initially Coleco planned to sell 500,000 units in 1983. It only managed to produce about 100,000 units that year, and the defect rate was alarmingly high. Coleco claimed 10 percent of the systems were defective, but retailers reported higher rates than that. One store manager told
Creative Computing
magazine that consumers returned five of six units he sold.
The
video game crash of 1983
was an opportunity for the Adam, with some consumer interest shifting from consoles to computers. But Coleco couldn’t deliver enough product fast enough and what it did deliver was flawed, so it couldn’t capitalize. Meanwhile, Commodore had sorted out its production issues and sold 3 million C-64s that year.
Design flaws
The Adam’ digital data packs looked just like audio cassettes, but were faster than the cassette-based solutions other 8-bit computers used. But they had reliability problems and weren’t as fast as a disk drive.
Even when the computer worked, it was less than ideal. The storage device was faster than Commodore’s or Atari’s tape drives. But it was slower than a disk drive. The Adam’s data packs had a tendency to unravel. Worse yet, if you had one in or near the drive when you turned the system on, the magnetic field would erase the tape inside.

data.author: fidotron
data.article_summary: Anysphere团队宣布获得9亿美元融资，估值达99亿美元，投资方包括Thrive、Accel、Andressen Horowitz和DST。其产品Cursor年经常性收入（ARR）超过5亿美元，被超过一半的福布斯500强企业使用，包括NVIDIA、Uber和Adobe。此轮融资将用于推进AI编程研究，实现构建更优编程方式的目标。团队对当前进展感到兴奋，并准备全力推进这项研究。

• aduffy认为，Cursor通过融资获得的巨额资金可能会用于扩大用户群、开发自主的基础代码模型以及进军企业市场，可能通过与咨询公司合作或直接与竞争对手如Accenture对抗。但aduffy对公司能否在基础模型上超越Big 3（OpenAI、Google、Anthropic）持怀疑态度。

• bix6关注的是Cursor的估值和市场上的其他收购案比较，并提到其客户支持问题，显示出对公司运营效率的关心。

• a13n预测开发者将回到VS Code，认为与微软直接竞争特别是在开发者+AI领域不是一个好局面，表达了对微软作为强大竞争对手的担忧。

• stonecharioteer对Cursor在短时间内从B轮到C轮融资的速度感到困惑，质疑公司融资速度是否合理。

• habosa指出Cursor可能需要开发自己的模型以确保长期生存，特别是在面对OpenAI、Anthropic和Google可能切断其资源的情况下，并提到Cursor拒绝被OpenAI收购的传闻。

• justmarc认为AI领域内的公司将面临激烈的生存竞争，暗示市场可能即将进入整合期。

• xiphias2分享了自己的使用体验，从Cursor转向Codex web界面，并预测随着模型增强，开发流程将转向基于pull request的开发模式。

• bahmboo表示对Roo Code的喜爱，并对Cursor等其他工具持观望态度，显示出对不同工具的比较和选择上的犹豫。

• mythz乐见Cursor的巨额融资将有助于维持市场价格竞争，但自己因习惯于现有IDE而不打算尝试Cursor，显示出对现有工具的忠诚。

• adwn对Cursor快速融资的资金使用和市场竞争表示关注，质疑资金使用的有效性及市场竞争策略。

• gsibble对Cursor近期多次融资表示印象深刻，但也暗示对融资频繁的疑惑。

• drx对Cursor由团队而非CEO发布融资消息表示赞赏，认为这是有趣且可能值得推广的做法。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点之一是Cursor是否需要开发自主模型以确保长期生存，特别是在面对强大竞争对手时。
• 另一个值得注意的讨论点是对市场竞争及估值的关注，尤其是与其他类似公司的收购和融资案例的比较。
• 用户体验和工具选择的讨论也显示出Cursor在实际使用中的竞争压力和用户忠诚度挑战。

data.title: Researchers find a way to make the HIV virus visible within white blood cells
data.author: colinprince
data.article_summary: 研究人员在寻找HIV治愈方法方面取得了突破，发现了一种迫使病毒从隐藏的白细胞中显现的新方法，为彻底清除体内HIV铺平了道路。HIV能够藏匿于特定白细胞内，使得病毒在体内形成潜伏库，难以被免疫系统或药物清除。来自墨尔本彼得·多尔蒂感染与免疫研究所的团队利用mRNA技术，通过特制的脂肪泡将mRNA送入隐藏HIV的细胞，使其揭示病毒。这种新型的脂质纳米颗粒（LNP X）成功解决了此前无法将mRNA送入此类细胞的难题。尽管还需进一步研究以确定揭示病毒是否足以让免疫系统消灭它，但这一发现为HIV治愈带来了新希望。研究还在早期阶段，距离临床应用还需多年研究和试验。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：HIV治疗的新方法及其潜在应用和限制

不同观点：
• [w10-1] 认为该研究虽然展示了通过封装mRNA激活潜伏HIV细胞的方法，但以往类似尝试均未成功清除病毒库。该方法可能更多是验证一种技术的可行性，而非直接用于治愈HIV。还提到HIV治疗的高昂成本使其成为长期治疗，药物公司可能更关注资金支持。
  
• [blindriver] 认为制药公司缺乏治愈HIV的动力，因为治愈性治疗不如长期的月度治疗（如Ozempic）对 Wall Street 有吸引力。引用Gilead治愈丙型肝炎却遭到批评的例子，暗示经济利益影响HIV治愈的研发。

• [bawolff] 提出该方法是否可以应用于其他潜伏性病毒，如带状疱疹或疱疹病毒，表明该技术可能具有更广泛的应用前景。

• [kylehotchkiss] 提到该技术在HIV上的成功是否可以延伸至其他疾病，如结核病和麻风病，表明了对技术扩展应用的期待。

• [istjohn] 引用Tomáš Hanke教授的观点，质疑将RNA导入白细胞的难度，并认为希望通过这种方式触及所有潜伏HIV的细胞“ merely a dream”（仅仅是个梦想），暗示该方法的实际效果可能有限。

• [user____name] 提到另一个近期的突破，提供额外研究支持讨论，表明科学界在不断取得进展。

• [hackernoops] 简单表示该发展是积极的，没有深入讨论，但持乐观态度。

补充讨论：
- 经济利益与HIV治愈研究之间的关系是一个争议焦点，尤其是制药公司是否真正愿意投入资源寻找治愈方案，还是更倾向于维持长期治疗方案。
- 该技术是否能广泛应用于其他潜伏性病毒疾病也是讨论的一个扩展方向。
- 不同评论对该研究实际效果的预期存在分歧，部分评论持怀疑态度，而其他评论则较为乐观。

争议焦点：制药公司是否真正有动力去治愈HIV，以及该新方法的实际应用效果。

An illustration of HIV virus particles. The virus has the ability to conceal itself within certain white blood cells.
Illustration: Ruslanas Baranauskas/Science Photo Library/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
An illustration of HIV virus particles. The virus has the ability to conceal itself within certain white blood cells.
Illustration: Ruslanas Baranauskas/Science Photo Library/Getty Images
Global development
Breakthrough in search for HIV cure leaves researchers ‘overwhelmed’
Exclusive: Melbourne team demonstrates way to make the virus visible within white blood cells, paving the way to fully clear it from the body
Supported by
About this content
Kat Lay
Global health correspondent
Thu 5 Jun 2025 01.00 EDT
Last modified on Fri 6 Jun 2025 00.25 EDT
Share
A cure for HIV could be a step closer after researchers found a new way to force the virus out of hiding inside human cells.
The virus’s ability to conceal itself inside certain white blood cells has been one of the main challenges for scientists looking for a cure. It means there is a reservoir of the HIV in the body, capable of reactivation, that neither the immune system nor drugs can tackle.
Now researchers from the Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity in Melbourne, have demonstrated a way to make the virus visible, paving the way to fully clear it from the body.
It is based on mRNA technology, which came to prominence during the Covid-19 pandemic
when it was used in vaccines
made by Moderna and Pfizer/BioNTech.
In a
paper published in Nature Communications
, the researchers have shown for the first time that mRNA can be delivered into the cells where HIV is hiding, by encasing it in a tiny, specially formulated fat bubble. The mRNA then instructs the cells to reveal the virus.
Globally, there are
almost 40 million people
living with HIV, who must take medication for the rest of their lives in order to suppress the virus and ensure they do not develop symptoms or transmit it. For many it remains deadly, with UNAids figures suggesting one person died of HIV every minute in 2023.
It was “previously thought impossible” to deliver mRNA to the type of white blood cell that is home to HIV, said Dr Paula Cevaal, research fellow at the Doherty Institute and co-first author of the study, because those cells did not take up the fat bubbles, or lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), used to carry it.
The team have developed a new type of LNP that those cells will accept, known as LNP X. She said: “Our hope is that this new nanoparticle design could be a new pathway to an HIV cure.”
When a colleague first presented test results at the lab’s weekly meeting, Cevaal said, they seemed too good to be true.
“We sent her back into the lab to repeat it, and she came back the next week with results that were equally good. So we had to believe it. And of course, since then, we’ve repeated it many, many, many more times.
“We were overwhelmed by how [much of a] night and day difference it was – from not working before, and then all of a sudden it was working. And all of us were just sitting gasping like, ‘wow’.”
Further research will be needed to determine whether revealing the virus is enough to allow the body’s immune system to deal with it, or whether the technology will need to be combined with other therapies to eliminate HIV from the body.
The study is laboratory based and was carried out in cells donated by HIV patients. The path to using the technology as part of a cure for patients is long, and would require successful tests in animals followed by safety trials in humans, likely to take years, before efficacy trials could even begin.
“In the field of biomedicine, many things eventually don’t make it into the clinic – that is the unfortunate truth; I don’t want to paint a prettier picture than what is the reality,” stressed Cevaal. “But in terms of specifically the field of HIV cure, we have never seen anything close to as good as what we are seeing, in terms of how well we are able to reveal this virus.
“So from that point of view, we’re very hopeful that we are also able to see this type of response in an animal, and that we could eventually do this in humans.”
Dr Michael Roche of the University of Melbourne and co-senior author of the research, said the discovery could have broader implications beyond HIV, with the relevant white blood cells also involved in other diseases including cancers.
Dr Jonathan Stoye, a retrovirologist and emeritus scientist at the Francis Crick Institute, who was not involved in the study, said the approach taken by the Melbourne team appeared be a major advance on existing strategies to force the virus out of hiding, but further studies would be needed to determine how best to kill it after that.
He added: “Ultimately, one big unknown remains. Do you need to eliminate the entire reservoir for success or just the major part? If just 10% of the latent reservoir survives will that be sufficient to seed new infection? Only time will

data.title: VPN providers in France ordered to block pirate sports IPTV
data.author: gasull
data.article_summary: 法国体育法典第L. 333-10条允许权利人请求封锁涉嫌严重且反复侵权的盗版网站。在Canal+投诉后，2024年，Cloudflare和Google的第三方DNS解析服务被法院要求协助封锁盗版网站。2025年2月，Canal+和其子公司对NordVPN、CyberGhost、ProtonVPN、ExpressVPN和Surfshark提起诉讼，指控这些VPN用户访问在法国非法的体育赛事盗版流媒体。法院驳回了VPN提供商的多项异议，认为根据法国体育法典第L. 333-10条和数字服务法，VPN提供商有责任采取措施阻止用户访问盗版网站。法院命令这些VPN公司在三天内采取必要措施，封锁指定盗版网站，直至2025年5月25日赛季结束。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：体育赛事流媒体的合法性、访问限制、以及VPN的使用在体育内容盗版问题中的角色。

不同观点：
• [MentatOnMelange] 认为体育行业的顾客愿意为观看比赛支付高额费用，但行业本身却通过地域限制等手段阻止人们合法观看，导致盗版问题。盗版与潜在利润之间的关系并非精确科学，很多盗版行为是因为人们无法在所在地区合法观看比赛。

• [space_firmware] 关注欧洲法院为防止体育流媒体盗版所采取的法律工具，认为这些工具可能为未来互联网的审查和控制提供基础。之前互联网服务提供商和VPN提供商可以抵制政府的审查要求，但现在这些工具的实施使得抵制变得更加困难，且该工具可能会扩展到体育领域之外。

• [Workaccount2] 建议通过合理定价和简化访问方式来减少盗版。他们指出，流媒体服务通过提供便宜和便捷的服务有效减少了盗版，但体育赛事在很多地区依然存在访问困难和高成本的问题。

• [Beijinger] 分享了个人使用VPN的经验，推荐了一些正在促销的VPN服务，但对其在不同操作系统下的表现持保留态度。

• [notorandit] 警告VPN用户在订阅服务时要三思，指出VPN提供商受到本国法律约束，可能会被执法机构要求提供用户信息。因此，除非用于合法活动，否则尝试规避法律是不明智的。

• [Disposal8433] 对法院禁止访问某些流媒体网站表示嘲讽，认为与Facebook等大公司相比，这些针对体育流媒体的举措显得虚伪且缺乏一致性。

• [mitkebes] 探讨了双重VPN是否能绕过地域限制，认为通过使用两个VPN可以绕过单个VPN的封锁，因为法律只适用于某一地区的用户。

• [kinow] 提供了西班牙类似情况的参考，指出这种做法在其他地区早已存在。

• [FirmwareBurner] 表达了对盗版体育广播列表的兴趣，似乎更关注如何获取盗版内容。

• [retrodaredevil] 讨论了VPN提供商遵守法院命令时的具体实施方式，特别是是否仅在DNS层面进行封锁，并提出使用未被审查的DNS提供商的可能性。

• [eloisant] 提到ProtonVPN可能需要在瑞士法院确认后才会遵守相关法律命令，暗示不同国家的法律适用差异。

• [fifteen1506] 认为虽然目前能找到绕过封锁的方法，但未来这些方法可能会变得像在PS5上安装Linux一样复杂，并担心未经认证的操作系统可能因此被封锁。

补充讨论：
- 评论中对VPN的使用及其法律风险有较多讨论，部分用户关注如何规避封锁，而另一些用户则提醒使用VPN的潜在法律问题。
- 对体育赛事流媒体的合法访问和定价策略的批评较为集中，用户普遍认为高价和地域限制是导致盗版的主要原因。
- 欧洲法院和其他地区类似案例的比较显示出这一问题具有国际性和复杂性。

44201857.article_content:
Major VPN Providers Ordered to Block Pirate Sports Streaming Sites
Article L. 333-10 of the French Sport Code enables rightsholders to request blocking measures against named pirate sites if they can demonstrate “serious and repeated infringement” of their exploitation rights.
To prevent pirate sites from being accessed on French soil, rightsholders may request that “all proportionate measures” are implemented by
any
online entity in a position to help. The scope of
Article L. 333-10
was always meant to be broad.
The first logical targets were local ISPs which easily fell within scope. Then, when inevitable circumvention raised its head, utilizing infrastructure beyond the reach of regular ISPs, Article L. 333-10 already had that covered.
Following a Canal+ complaint, use of third party DNS resolvers at Cloudflare and Google
headed to court in 2024
. Both were labeled intermediaries by the Court, and under the still unstressed scope of Article L. 333-10, both were considered capable of contributing to the suppression of piracy.
Canal+ / LFP Target Major VPN Providers
Having effectively added public DNS resolvers to the French blocking machine, attention turned to the next targets. In February 2025, it emerged that Groupe Canal + and Société d’édition de Canal Plus (SECP) had
filed a case
in November 2024 against NordVPN, CyberGhost, ProtonVPN, ExpressVPN, and Surfshark.
The Canal companies alleged that “numerous” websites, accessible from within France, illegally streamed matches from various sporting competitions to which they hold the rights.
Since the VPNs’ subscribers were among those viewing the infringing streams, the Canal companies asked the court to compel the providers to implement “all measures likely to prevent access [to the illegal streams] from French territory,” including in all French overseas territories, “by any effective means”.
The VPN providers objected to the application on various grounds. Nord and Surfshark requested a declaration that the Canal companies lacked standing to act; as such, their application should be declared inadmissible. Proton sought a similar declaration while noting that the company lacked the ability to defend the requested blocking measures. The same assertion was made by CyberGhost and Express; all argued that Article L. 333-10 does not apply to VPN providers.
Other objections concerned jurisdiction and whether French law is compatible with EU legislation. CyberGhost and Express suggested a stay of proceedings pending a response from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in the Dutch case,
AFS et al
.
Court Rejects VPN Providers’ Objections
In its decision published Thursday, the Court found that matters concerning the CJEU would have no impact on the current case. Calls for the Canal companies’ application to be declared inadmissible due to a lack of standing, were also dismissed, while a review of the allocation of rights pertaining to the various sports competitions raised no concerns.
Arguments that the VPN providers had no standing to defend themselves, due to Article L. 333-10 of the French Sports Code being inapplicable to VPN providers, fared no better.
The court notes that Article L.333-10 does not impose any restrictions on the targeted entity, adding that VPN providers are expressly covered under the Digital Services Act.
“Blocking such a service for certain domain names means that the provider of this service prevents its users from accessing the disputed domain names when using their VPN tool. Internet users using these virtual private networks would therefore no longer be able to access the disputed sites through this intermediary,” the decision reads.
“Consequently, the defendant companies, in their capacity as providers of virtual private network services, are technical intermediaries capable of contributing to remedying the harm that Groupe Canal+, SECP and Canal+ Rights claim to have suffered.”
Blocking Order Issued
The Court’s instructions and the full list of domains can be found below.

44201857.article_summary: 法国体育法典第L. 333-10条允许权利人请求封锁涉嫌严重且反复侵权的盗版网站。在Canal+投诉后，2024年，Cloudflare和Google的第三方DNS解析服务被法院要求协助封锁盗版网站。2025年2月，Canal+和其子公司对NordVPN、CyberGhost、ProtonVPN、ExpressVPN和Surfshark提起诉讼，指控这些VPN用户访问在法国非法的体育赛事盗版流媒体。法院驳回了VPN提供商的多项异议，认为根据法国体育法典第L. 333-10条和数字服务法，VPN提供商有责任采取措施阻止用户访问盗版网站。法院命令这些VPN公司在三天内采取必要措施，封锁指定盗版网站，直至2025年5月25日赛季结束。

- 对体育赛事流媒体的合法访问和定价策略的批评较为集中，用户普遍认为高价和地域限制是导致盗版的主要原因。

data.title: A year of funded FreeBSD development
data.author: cperciva
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：FreeBSD操作系统的发展现状、驱动支持、企业资助情况及其在Unix生态中的定位。

不同观点：
• msdrigg分享了FreeBSD在2024年初启动过程变慢的问题，并通过提交历史追踪到根磁盘大小增加的提交。他通过将磁盘大小增加到8 GB恢复了性能，但其根本原因不明。
• AndyKelley强调了FreeBSD在Zig语言项目中的新支持，包括自动构建和跨平台编译功能，鼓励更多项目支持FreeBSD。
• net01提到BSD基金会在笔记本电脑项目上的投入，特别是实现S0ix睡眠状态等功能。
• tiffanyh对cperciva同时管理Tarsnap和FreeBSD工作表示钦佩。
• ksec批评亚马逊、谷歌、苹果和Meta等大公司对FreeBSD的支持不足，尽管这些公司从开源软件中获益，但 sponsorship 贡献较少。
• xedrac尝试用FreeBSD作为家庭网关服务器，但由于10 GbE网卡缺少驱动，最终选择了Nix。
• nithssh提到FreeBSD曾对Atheros WiFi卡的支持优于Linux，但现代混合CPU架构下调度器表现不佳。
• commandersaki好奇EC2上FreeBSD的主要用户是谁。
• johnnyjeans询问FreeBSD在Unix领域的独特定位，为什么不选择OpenBSD、NetBSD或Linux。
• LAC-Tech认为FreeBSD的开发状况令人担忧，操作系统复杂性需要全职的发布经理，而不仅仅是一年的兼职支持。

补充讨论：
• SSLy提到了一个编码问题，虽然没有详细说明。
• 讨论中多次提及企业资助问题，特别是大公司对开源项目的贡献不平衡，成为争议焦点。
• 不同用户对FreeBSD的驱动支持和在现代硬件上的表现有不同看法，特别是与Linux和其他BSD变种的比较。
• FreeBSD在特定技术（如ZFS、Nvidia驱动、ELF等）上的支持被认为是其在Unix领域中的优势，但也有人质疑其相对于Linux的独特性。

data.title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Limitations of Reasoning LLMs [pdf]
data.author: amrrs
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：大型语言模型（LLMs）及语言模型推理能力（LRMs）的局限性与潜力

不同观点：
• **对LLMs能力的困惑与思考**：[throwaway71271] 认为LLMs使用语言的方式让人类感到困惑，尽管理解其内部机制，但其能力仍然像魔法一样难以捉摸。他强调需要更多努力去理解如何利用这些模型并构建更强大的系统。
• **复杂性与经济价值的关系**：[curious_cat_163] 对将复杂性映射到经济价值的讨论感兴趣，认为需要超越 puzzle 环境的评估方式，但仍需保持任务复杂性的可控性。
• **对AI发展的批评与怀疑**：[jbentley1] 质疑Apple在AI研发方面的投入，暗示其可能在忽视AI的重要性。[actinium226] 提到了AI发展中的"Gartner hype cycle"，暗示对AGI即将到来的过度期待。
• **LLMs与传统计算方法的结合**：[teleforce] 认为LLMs/LRMs在精确计算方面有局限，建议结合逻辑、优化和约束编程等方法来提升其能力。
• **LLMs在不同任务中的表现**：[thomasahle] 指出LLMs在允许编写代码的情况下可以完美解决某些任务，质疑研究中对LLMs能力的限制是否合理。[JusticeJuice] 对LLMs在不同复杂任务中的表现研究结果表示认可。
• **LLMs的思考模式与改进方向**：[cdrini] 认为当前LLMs在处理复杂问题时需要像人类一样能够在思考过程中进行迭代和修改，而不是一次性输出结果。[benlivengood] 强调持续进步，认为前言LLMs在性能上远超旧模型。
• **对研究定义的质疑**：[nialv7] 对研究中未明确定义“推理”、“可泛化性”和“模式匹配”等概念表示不满，认为需要先明确这些定义才能更好地理解研究结果。
• **对研究结果的解释**：[danck] 认为LLMs在复杂任务中失败是因为token预算不足，只要扩大token预算就能提高其能力。
• **对LLMs局限性的接受**：[esafak] 认为LLMs和人类一样有局限性，指出即使是人类也没有解决许多开放性问题。
• **对LLMs过度工程化的担忧**：[beneboy] 提到Claude在寻找正确解决方案时可能会过度工程化，研究结果揭示了这一问题。

补充讨论：
• **对AGI未来发展的讨论**：[antics] 认为当前模型是“全知却愚钝”的，并质疑这种状态是否会持续下去，认为需要更尖锐的分析来推动不同观点之间的对话。
• **历史视角与AI研发的经济驱动**：[d4rkn0d3z] 从历史角度回顾AI发展，指出当前AI研究更多受到资本驱动，而非科学探索，强调解决硬问题的重要性。

争议焦点：
• **LLMs是否具备真正的推理能力**：一些评论质疑LLMs是否能够进行真正的推理，还是仅仅依赖模式匹配。[nialv7] 强调需要明确定义和人类推理的对比。
• **LLMs在复杂任务中的表现是否可以通过简单扩展解决**：[danck] 认为通过增加token预算可以解决复杂任务中的问题，而[cdrini] 认为需要更类似于人类的思考和迭代过程。

总结：讨论围绕LLMs和LRMs的能力与局限性展开，涉及其在不同任务中的表现、改进方向以及与传统计算方法的结合。同时，对AI发展中的经济驱动和AGI未来发展的讨论也占据一定篇幅。

data.title: Wendelstein 7-X sets new fusion record
data.author: doener
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕核聚变研究进展及其未来潜力的不同观点和讨论。

不同观点：
• [支持与乐观]  
  - [ChuckMcM] 对核聚变工程进展持乐观态度，赞赏研究团队不断实现工程目标，并对未来五年内建成能源生产型仿星器（stellarator）充满信心。
  - [mrbluecoat] 赞赏科学成就和工程美学，感叹真空容器内部结构的复杂工程。

• [实用主义与怀疑态度]  
  - [Synaesthesia] 对核聚变持怀疑态度，认为应该更多关注核裂变和可再生能源（如太阳能和风能），并指出中国和俄罗斯在核能领域的领先地位。

• [技术实现与理论模型的讨论]  
  - [ninetyninenine] 质疑为何数学建模和模拟尚未提供完美的设计，并询问是否缺乏有效的数学模型，认为需要实际建造和测试才能验证设计。

• [对不同核聚变技术的比较与预测]  
  - [jablongo] 对未来十年内不同核聚变技术的成功可能性进行排名，认为仿星器可能在2060年成为主流设计，但在近期内更看好托卡马克和Helion的设计。

补充讨论：
• [对具体技术指标的解释]  
  - [Robotbeat] 强调核聚变研究中的关键指标——等离子体“三重积”，并解释了Lawson准则及其在不同核聚变方法比较中的应用。

• [提供信息来源]  
  - [_Microft] 提供官方网站声明以支持讨论。
  - [s1artibartfast] 提供存档和替代信息来源以供参考。

• [对人工智能与核聚变进展的类比]  
  - [ipnon] 将人工智能的发展轨迹与核聚变进行类比，认为两者都存在预期与现实的差距。

争议焦点：
• 核聚变技术是否能在短期内实现实际应用，还是应该更多地关注其他能源解决方案。  
• 数学建模和模拟在核聚变设计中的局限性以及实际建造和测试的必要性。

data.title: A Rippling Townhouse Facade by Alex Chinneck Takes a Seat in a London Square
data.author: surprisetalk
data.article_summary: 英国艺术家Alex Chinneck在伦敦Clerkenwell设计周上展出了新作《A week at the knees》。这件雕塑位于 Charterhouse Square，重塑了一栋经典乔治亚风格联排别墅的外墙，使其下两层仿佛波浪般“坐”在路径上，给人一种轻盈、玩味的视觉效果。雕塑高5米，重12吨，由320米再生钢和7,000块砖制成，厚度仅15厘米，呈现出厚重建筑结构与轻盈姿态的对比。该作品与多家英国公司合作完成，结合了定制的钢梁、弯曲的窗户和砖块，并在细节上融入了周围历史环境的元素，如排水管和拱门前门两侧的灯具。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：[对某个建筑或雕塑作品的不同看法，包括其与自然的关系、工艺难度以及对作品的感受]

不同观点：
• [impossiblefork] 认为该建筑（或雕塑）虽然是有趣的，但觉得砖结构是对自然的一种人为强加，更喜欢原本生长在那里的草木。他觉得如果这是一个隧道可能会更好。
• [hn_throwaway_99] 对作品的工艺表示赞赏，特别是窗户的部分。他认为在曲面上制作和安装弯曲的窗框和窗格非常困难，而作品中实现了这一点显示出对细节的极致关注，增加了整体的 illusion 效果，使其看起来像一块可折叠的地毯。
• [adammarples] 没有表达对作品的具体看法，只是询问作品的位置，显示出对作品背景信息的兴趣。
• [egypturnash] 以轻松的语气表示想要玩一个与此作品相关的滑板游戏，表现出对作品的娱乐性联想。
• [readthenotes1] 对作品的经济成本提出质疑，使用“More money than sense”这一短语来表达对资源投入的怀疑，并通过文字游戏（“pense”代替“sense”）增加评论的幽默感。

补充讨论：
• 争议的焦点可能在于作品是否与自然和谐共存。impossiblefork 认为这是对自然的人为干预，而其他评论没有直接回应这一观点，更多关注作品的工艺和娱乐价值。
• hn_throwaway_99 对工艺细节的分析提供了技术性的视角，强调了作品在设计和执行上的难度和精细程度。
• 其他评论如 adammparples 和 egypturnash 更多的是对作品的个人兴趣和娱乐联想，没有涉及深层次的批评或分析。

Photos by Charles Emerson. All images courtesy of Alex Chinneck Studio, shared with permission
A Rippling Townhouse Facade by Alex Chinneck Takes a Seat in a London Square
May 22, 2025
Art
Design
Kate Mothes
Share
Pin
Email
Bookmark
It takes a real knack for design to make something as hefty and industrial as steel and bricks appear weightless or even playful. But British artist
Alex Chinneck
(
previously
) is no stranger to monumental projects that reimagine urban infrastructure and buildings into striking public installations.
As part of London’s
Clerkenwell Design Week
, Chinneck unveiled “A week at the knees,” a new sculpture in Charterhouse Square that takes its cue from
an iconic predecessor
. The artist installed the “From the Knees of my Nose to the Belly of my Toes” in 2013 on a dilapidated townhouse in Margate, appearing as though the entire front of the building had simply slid right off. On view through June in London, his new work boasts a frame made from 320 meters of repurposed steel and 7,000 bricks.
“A week at the knees” playfully anthropomorphizes a classic Georgian facade, with its lower two levels rippling over a pathway as if seated in the park with its knees up. London is famous for its green squares and gardens, and Chinneck’s work invites visitors to pass through a unique portal that calls upon the history of its surroundings, complete with downspout and lamps flanking the arched front door.
Chinneck fabricated the sculpture in collaboration with numerous British companies to source and create bespoke steel beams, curving windows, and bricks. At five meters tall and weighing 12 tons, the piece mimics a life-size building while sporting a thickness of only 15 centimeters. The effect lends itself to the experience of a hefty, architectonic structure with a graceful, lightweight personality.

website
and
Instagram
.

data.title: Workhorse LLMs: Why Open Source Models Dominate Closed Source for Batch Tasks
data.author: cmogni1
data.article_summary: 文章主要讨论了为何在批量任务中，开源大型语言模型（LLM）比闭源模型更具优势。尽管在高端智能任务中，闭源模型如GPT、Claude和Gemini仍占主导地位，但对于许多常见业务任务（如文本分类、摘要、数据提取等），开源模型表现同样出色，且成本更低。文章比较了开源和闭源模型的性能和成本，指出对于“工作马”模型（workhorse models），开源模型提供了更高的性价比，尤其是在使用批量推理服务时，能实现显著的成本节约。文章还介绍了如何使用人工智能指数（Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index）来评估模型性能，并提供了开源替代模型的推荐及相应的成本节约预期。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：对不同AI编码模型的性价比和实用性进行评估

不同观点：
• jbellis认为Grok 3 mini和DeepSeek V3是值得尝试的最便宜的编码模型，分别适用于不同场景。然而，他指出，作者通过将人工智能分析得分除以混合每token成本来评估模型的方法存在问题，因为大多数任务有一个智能“底线”，低于这个底线，模型的表现就不会成功。他还提到，去除超级便宜的4B OSS模型的非常高分结果后，其余模型远不及Flash 2.0和2.5，尤其是在特定领域任务中。

• delichon强调了选择模型时的情境依赖性，建议根据需求设置不同的按钮（如<dumber>和<smarter>），并以$/M tokens为单位。他还希望有一个功能可以将特定提示发送到“[x]批次”并稍后通过电子邮件发送答案。这种灵活性可以满足不同任务需求。

• ramesh31认为Flash模型目前价格极其便宜，因此自托管模型（如Grok 3 mini）仅在处理敏感数据时才有必要。

Workhorse LLMs: Why Open Source Models Dominate Closed Source for Batch Tasks
Sutro Team
Jun 6, 2025
As LLMs become more prolific, weâve noticed that teams still reach for closed sourced models like GPT, Claude, and Gemini for nearly every task. While this may have been the right call a year ago, teams today are unknowingly missing out on huge cost savings and performance gains by not considering open source alternatives.
It is true that at the frontier of intelligence, the most powerful closed source LLMs dominate their open source counterparts. However, many common tasks for LLMs donât require PhD level reasoning. Instead, they require a workhorse LLM: something thatâs reliable for low-to-medium difficulty tasks â things like classification, summarization, and data extraction.
Not only are there suitable replacements for closed source workhorses like GPT-4o-mini, but the equivalent replacements are often less expensive
and
more intelligent. When latency isnât an issue, open source models have an even larger edge for cost savings if running jobs in bulk through a batch inference provider like Sutro.
In this guide, we compare the performance and cost of workhorse models. After the analysis, we provide a handy conversion chart that helps you pick the best open source replacement for the closed source models you may have used along with the cost savings you should expect by making the switch.
How Do Open Source LLMs Stack Up Against Closed Source LLMs?
A common question organizations ask us is how the cost and performance of open source models stack up against closed source models. To answer this question, itâs best to divide the field into two categories: frontier models and workhorse models.
Frontier models are the biggest, most capable models. They promise emergent capabilities, generalization across tasks, and the ability to handle complex context and instructions.
At the frontier, closed source models like Claude Opus 4.0, OpenAIâs o3 model, and Gemini 2.5 Pro dominate. However, open source models like Qwen 3 235B-A22B and DeepSeek R1 (and the to-be-released R2) are closing the gap quickly.
The closed providers also provide smaller, less-expensive models. These include GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Claude Haiku 3.5. Many companies choose to adopt these models to save on costs when running tasks that require less general reasoning capabilities.  We refer to these as âworkhorseâ models, and believe that for this class of model open-source dominates.
Workhorse models are extremely adept at most common business tasks, including:
Structured Extraction:
Turning free form-text or images into JSON format and analytics-ready datasets.
Summarizing Text:
Turning large documents or conversations into bullet points or summaries.
Answering Questions:
Doing Q&A that doesnât require complex reasoning on your documents.
Sentiment Analysis:
Determining how positive, negative, or neutral a given text is.
Generating Synthetic Data:
Creating datasets from scratch to power fine-tuning or improving RAG systems.
Data Extraction And Organization:
Finding and extracting particular pieces of information from unstructured text.
Classification:
Sorting text into categories specific to your applications.
Running Evals:
Evaluating the robustness of your prompts using techniques like LLM-as-a-judge and metric scoring.
Most organizations already use models like GPT-4o-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash to do these tasks to speed up inference and keep costs low. As we demonstrate below, equivalent open source LLMs can get you the same or better performance, sometimes with huge cost savings, especially if using a batch API like Sutro.
How Open Source LLMs For Common Business Tasks Stack Up
Figuring out how well an LLM performs is tricky. Most model creators game benchmarks by training for the test and testing using prompts that are carefully crafted to perform well. Nonetheless, because model providers are all trying to game the system in similar ways, benchmarks still give us a heuristic for
relative
capabilities.
To determine which workhorse open source models are likely a good replacement performance and cost wise for closed source models you have probably used, we will use Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index. The Intelligence Index is a weighted average of benchmarks across many tasks. Using this lets us not overweight any one benchmark and helps us get the heuristic we are looking for.
Additionally, we pulled together the average cost per token for common workhorse tasks. We used a 10:1 blended ratio of input-to-output tokens for non-thinking models, which we calculated from internal metrics. For models with thinking mode, we budgeted 2k thinking tokens, adjusting the blended ratio to 3:2.
Finally, we calculated a performance-to-cost ratio - a "bang for buck" measurement - using the Artificial Analysis Index scores, giving us a unified metric with which to com

data.title: Medieval Africans had a unique process for purifying gold with glass (2019)
data.author: mooreds
data.article_summary: 在马里的Tadmekka，考古学家萨姆·尼克松发现了11世纪用于铸造金币的模具碎片，这些模具中留有高纯度金滴和玻璃碎片。研究表明，中世纪西非人使用了一种创新的金精炼方法，他们将金与玻璃混合，利用玻璃溶解杂质，从而提取出纯金。与欧洲同时期的杯化法不同，这种方法显示了当地工匠的创造性和对材料特性的深刻理解。玻璃是回收自破损器皿，体现了Tadmekka作为跨撒哈拉商路重要节点的贸易活动。研究团队通过实验重现了这一古老技术，验证了其巧妙和复杂性。

补充讨论：
• gregschlom感慨对中世纪非洲历史缺乏了解，这引发了对非洲中世纪历史知识的反思。
• goodmunky和AlecSchueler对使用“非洲人”一词提出质疑，认为非洲地域广阔且多样，使用这一泛称可能不准确，这涉及对文化与地理术语准确性的讨论。
• kleton提供了具体技术名词“cupellation”（灰吹法）并指出罗马人曾使用类似技术，这为bcoates的疑问提供了可能的答案。
• bargle0关注金粉的纯度问题，进一步探讨了化学供应公司提供材料的质量。
• ChuckMcM询问是否有相关论文链接，显示出对技术细节和来源的兴趣。
• KolibriFly强调创新不一定来自大型机构，暗示对不同文化中技术创新的关注。
• dondakirme和detourdog对过程表示兴趣，尤其是其源于“玩火”的探索精神，这为讨论增加了历史技术发展的人文视角。

争议焦点：

44205599.article_content:
The coin mold fragments found in Tadmekka, Mali.
Photograph by Clare Britt, Courtesy The Block Museum of Art
In This Story
Destination Guide
Mali
1 Articles
7 Places
When Sam Nixon, an archaeologist
with the British Museum, excavated ancient coin molds in Tadmekka, Mali, in 2005, it triggered a several-year exploration of how medieval Africans purified the gold they were using for their currency. Nixon had
found
little droplets of highly refined gold left over in the molds—which have been dated to the 11th century—as well as curious fragments of glass. Now scientists have recreated the advanced process behind the purification method they used then.
“This is the first time in the archaeological record that we saw glass being used to be able to refine gold,” says Marc Walton, codirector of the
Center for Scientific Studies in the Arts
, a collaboration between Northwestern University and the Art Institute of Chicago. “The glass appeared to be material that was [actually] recycled glass materials … so it really shows the industriousness and creativity of the craftsmen, who understood the properties of gold and glass enough to [use them for] this process of refining gold.” The recycled glass materials were remnants of broken vessels. Tadmekka was a town right in the middle of the trans-Saharan caravan route, so Nixon uncovered several types of material culture that had to do with trade, namely molds for “bald dinar,” or coins that hadn’t been stamped with the name of a mint (or a 10th-century equivalent of one).
An illuminated atlas depicts Mansa Musa, emperor of Mali from 1312 to 1337, widely known for his vast vast wealth in the form of gold deposits.
Courtesy The Block Museum of Art
According to Walton, Europeans in the 10th and 11th centuries purified their gold through cupellation, a process in which lead is mixed with gold laced with impurities, and then heated in a furnace until the droplets of purer gold can be skimmed off. But in the case of medieval West Africans, “They were taking the ore and other raw materials from the river and mixing it with glass,” says Walton. Since gold is inert, it doesn’t fully dissolve into melted glass, while impurities and other materials do, making this “a really novel way of using recycled glass material.”
Walton’s team at the Center for Scientific Studies in the Arts replicates a lot of ancient technologies. To get to the bottom of how medieval Africans purified gold so successfully, they also made do with what their environment provided them. “We bought gold dust from a chemical supply company and then we mixed it with local Lake Michigan sand and then we made our own synthetic glass,” says Walton. “We heated it up, were able to dissolve the minerals in the sand, and were left behind with gold.”
Though Walton and his team updated this small-scale, bespoke process for purifying gold to modern times and adapted it to their environment in Illinois, their results show that the medieval Malian technique was both clever and sophisticated.

This British Colonial Report Offers a Rare Glimpse Into India's Historic Cannabis Cuisine
And a description of some very stoned canines.

data.title: Highly efficient matrix transpose in Mojo
data.author: timmyd
data.article_summary:
本文介绍了如何使用Mojo语言在Hopper架构上实现高效的矩阵转置内核。该内核实现了2775.49 GB/s的带宽，性能接近CUDA的2771.35 GB/s。文章详细描述了实现步骤，包括初始化TMA描述符、加载数据到共享内存、执行转置计算、以及将结果存储回全局内存。

主要步骤如下：

1. **初始化TMA描述符**：创建两个描述符，分别对应原始矩阵和转置矩阵。
2. **加载到共享内存**：使用TMA将数据异步复制到共享内存。
3. **计算转置**：在共享内存中完成矩阵转置。
4. **存储到GMEM**：将转置结果存储回全局内存。
5. **Swizzling优化**：通过调整描述符和索引实现进一步优化。

文章还提到，Mojo通过使用PTX API实现了比CUDA更高的带宽。Swizzling技术也被提及，提供了相关代码示例和详细解释的链接。最终的内核在性能上媲美CUDA，展示了Mojo在GPU计算上的潜力。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：关于Mojo编程语言及其在矩阵转置等操作中的应用和性能的讨论，包括其实用性、性能表现、以及是否适用于实际生产环境。

• daft_pink认为Mojo并不是一个真正的开放产品，其存在主要是为了推动Modular公司的利润，且在2025年使用授权编程语言是不切实际的。
• saagarjha分析了Mojo使用PTX API进行TMA传输的性能，认为虽然Mojo在某些情况下表现优于CUDA，但他不确定是否总是需要TMA来实现高速操作，尤其是在简单转置任务中。
• sestep质疑将矩阵转置与前后操作融合的效率，认为这种融合操作可能更常见且更高效。
• totalperspectiv关注粗粒度代码中的@parameter-for使用，询问这是否会导致代码体积增大，并表示从文章中学到了很多。
• londons_explore质疑是否有必要单独进行矩阵转置，建议将其与后续操作结合以提高效率。

• thunkingdeep指出“archive”可能应为“achieve”，质疑是否存在术语使用错误。
• melodyogonna好奇是否存在不使用Modular提供的高级抽象的理由。
• graycat提出快速矩阵转置可以通过改变索引算法实现，而不需要复杂的操作。
• arjvik质疑所谓14%的性能提升，认为实际提升仅为0.14%。
• vlan121强调Mojo编译器闭源是一个大问题。
• colesantiago询问是否有企业在生产环境中使用Mojo或招聘Mojo开发者。
• almostgotcaught赞同londons_explore的观点，认为不应单独编写转置内核，应融合其他操作。
• jsnell指出文章标题存在误导，实际性能提升仅为0.14%而非14%。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点之一是Mojo在矩阵转置任务中的实际性能提升是否如宣传所言，特别是0.14%与14%之间的差距。
• 另一个值得注意的点是Mojo编译器闭源问题及其对该语言广泛应用的影响。
• 讨论还涉及是否应将矩阵转置与其他操作结合以提高效率，以及高层次抽象和简单索引算法在矩阵操作中的应用。

data.title: What “working” means in the era of AI apps
data.author: Brysonbw
data.article_summary: 本文讨论了人工智能（AI）时代下初创公司的快速增长现象。相比于前AI时代，AI驱动的企业能够在更短时间内实现更高的收入，并以更快的速度完成融资轮次。例如，企业级公司在第一年内的中位收入已超过200万美元，消费者公司在八个月内达到420万美元收入。此外，顶级公司与一般公司之间的差距在扩大，顶级公司能持续加速增长。尽管收入增长迅速，其他指标如用户参与度和留存率依然重要。消费者公司也逐渐成为真正的创收业务，特别是在新模型发布时会出现显著增长。总体而言，AI应用时代为软件公司创造了前所未有的发展机会。

• [ednite] 从外部视角出发，指出当前AI预期过于高涨，尤其是非技术人群中的 hype。虽然当前的AI工具比以往的技术（如Y2K或dot-com泡沫）更具实质性，但最终决定AI是否会改变世界的是其财务可行性，而非单纯的创新或炒作。

What “Working” Means in the Era of AI Apps
Olivia Moore
and
Marc Andrusko
share
Copy Link
Email
X
LinkedIn
Facebook
Hacker News
WhatsApp
Flipboard
Reddit
Table of Contents
Table of Contents
Posted June 6, 2025
One of the most common refrains in the generative AI era is that “startups are growing faster than ever” — often with fewer resources. Some notable examples? Per company metrics, Lovable
hit
$50 million
in revenue in just six months, Cursor
reported
$100 million
in revenue in its first year, and Gamma
reached
$50 million
in revenue on less than $25 million raised.
But for the
average
AI company (not the top 0.1%), what does growth really look like? Pre-AI, a common benchmark for best-in-class enterprise startups was $1 million in ARR in its first 12 months. Consumer companies, by contrast, often delayed monetization well beyond their first year, typically waiting until they had built a base of millions (or tens of millions) of users to monetize through ads.
Based on data across hundreds of companies we’ve seen over the last 18 months, we can definitively say these metrics have shifted. Here’s what we’re seeing among the companies we’ve spent significant time with:
What does this mean for founders?
1. Faster revenue, faster rounds.
Our data backs up the idea that we’re in a new era of startup growth. The median enterprise company in our sample set reached more than $2 million in ARR in its first year, raising a Series A just nine months post-monetization. Median consumer companies performed even better, reaching $4.2 million in ARR and raising an A round within eight months. What was once considered “best in class” — the $0 to $1 million ARR ramp — is now on the lower end of growth we’re seeing.
Given the rapid growth both AI-native B2B and B2C companies are achieving between Seed and Series A, startups looking to raise venture capital need a strong velocity story. If not yet in live commercial traction, then certainly in shipping speed and product iteration. Speed is becoming a moat.
2. The gap between “good” and “exceptional” is growing.
While the bar has been raised across the board, top performers are really pulling away. Many of these breakout companies continue to pick up steam through their first year, rather than seeing growth start to slow (as we often saw in the pre-AI era). There’s demand from both enterprise and consumer users for great products, so it’s worth swinging for the fences.
It’s not just about revenue — other metrics still matter. When evaluating companies at the Series A stage, we often have no more than 12 months of usage and retention data. Later-stage financing rounds will likely rely more heavily on traditional software metrics; rapid top-line growth won’t be enough to compensate for low engagement or high churn.
3. Consumer companies are now…real (revenue-generating!) businesses.
Somewhat surprisingly, the revenue benchmarks for B2C are outpacing those for B2B. This is partially because consumer companies have a different “shape” now. One-third of the consumer companies in our sample raised significant funding to train their own models — and many see a massive revenue jump following new model releases. These spikes often resemble step function growth, which can later plateau until the next release.
While conversion to paid may be lower for generative AI B2C businesses compared to their pre-AI counterparts,
our data
suggests that once users
do
convert, they retain just as well.
*  *  *
TL;DR: Startups are working faster than ever, and both businesses and consumers are demonstrating high willingness to pay for new products. After combing through the data, we believe there’s never been a better time to build an application-layer software company.

data.title: Smalltalk, Haskell and Lisp
data.author: todsacerdoti
data.article_summary: 本文描述了作者在用Haskell、Common Lisp和Smalltalk三种语言解决同一问题时的体验。作者发现，尽管Haskell不一定是最实用或最合适的选择，但其代码简洁、清晰，且具有高度的模块化，特别适合其编程风格。相比之下，Smalltalk和Lisp的实现尽管功能相似，但前者显得冗长，后者则因语法和宏的使用让作者感觉像是在“欺骗”语言来实现目标，而非直接表达意图。作者尤其欣赏Haskell的`where`语法，可以轻松地将复杂操作分解为简单部分，使代码更具可读性和表达力。总体而言，作者认为Haskell在代码美学和编程体验上优于Lisp和Smalltalk。
data.comments_summary:

• [neilv] 认为Lisp代码看起来不错，提供了一个函数定义示例，并解释了其功能。该评论者对Lisp的函数式风格持积极态度。

• 最后，[transfire]提到可读性与习惯有关，并认为FORTH可能是一个例外，这为讨论提供了一个不同的视角。

Daniel's Blog
Home
Archives
Search
Feed
About
To assist with job interviews at the
NRAO
we recently wrote a small
“
contest” program. Without giving away the details, the crux of the problem is to read a file with a list of scans and calculate the amount of time it takes to move the dishes and perform the scans, and report it. Candidates are required to write this in Java, but that restriction does not apply to me, so I of course had to write it in three languages that are not Java: Haskell, Common Lisp and Smalltalk.
I expect to learn something, or at least reinforce an existing fact, by doing these sorts of language games, but this time I really wasn’t expecting what I found. I discovered that my enjoyment of Haskell is pretty much independent of Haskell’s appropriateness or usability. In fact, it is more attributable to the way I feel when using it, in contrast to everything else. Let me show you a piece of code:
-- | Perform a scan and produce the scan log for it.
performScan ∷ Scan → AntennaSimulator ScanLog
performScan scan = wrapDuration $ do
slewTime     ← moveTo  $ scanPosition scan  -- move to the scan's position
onSourceTime ← waitFor $ scanLength   scan  -- wait for the scan to finish
return $ Log scan onSourceTime slewTime
Somehow, the other languages I’ve used to implement this problem never arrived at a piece of code quite this beautiful. Compare to the Smalltalk:
Scan ≫ runWith: anAntenna
runWith: anAntenna
"Performs this scan on the supplied antenna."
| onSourceTime slewTime |
slewTime     := anAntenna moveTo: self position; lastActionDuration.
onSourceTime := anAntenna wait: self duration; lastActionDuration.
^ ScanResult withScan: self slewTime: slewTime onSourceTime: onSourceTime
And the Lisp:
(defun run-scan (antenna scan)
"Perform a scan on this antenna. Return a scan log."
(let* ((slew-time       (move-to antenna (scan-position scan)))
(on-source-time  (delay antenna (scan-length scan)))
(total-time      (+ on-source-time slew-time)))
(with-slots (last-duration) antenna
(setf last-duration total-time)
(make-scan-log scan slew-time on-source-time))))
Strangely, despite the similarity of the Smalltalk, I still find the Haskell shorter and clearer. It’s also more modular, though it doesn’t look like it. The
wrapDuration
command arranges for the next set of actions to count as one as far as the
lastActionDuration
is concerned, but does not interfere with usages of
lastActionDuration
within the wrapped action. I found this notion essentially impossible to port to the other languages. The Haskell version really feels more like a composable set of actions for driving the antenna, whereas the Smalltalk version never really stopped feeling like an arithmetic fabrication, and the abstraction leaked a lot in the Lisp version
The Lisp code is just atrocious. I was never really able to put my finger on what it is I dislike about Lisp before. It’s this: while Lisp code is often clever and interesting, it also
always
feels like I’m tricking Lisp into doing what I want, rather than simply expressing what I want.
Neither Lisp nor Smalltalk really lend themselves to my style. I realize now, that my style is to try to break everything down into the smallest piece, a piece that doesn’t look like work. Haskell encourages this style with the
where
syntax, which encourages you to say, X is really Y + Z, with Y being this and Z being that. This kind of thing:
-- | To calculate the time to move between two positions, we take
-- whichever is larger of the time to turn and the time to change
-- elevation.
timeToMoveTo ∷ Position → Position → Time
timeToMoveTo (sourceAz, sourceEl) (destAz, destEl) =
max rotationTime ascensionTime
where
rotationTime, ascensionTime ∷ Time
rotationTime  = timeToRotate sourceAz destAz
ascensionTime = timeToAscend sourceEl destEl
This almost doesn’t look like code to me. I would expect any programmer to be able to at least get some sense of what’s going on here, even without knowing Haskell. I don’t think I could say the same thing about this piece of Lisp:
(defun time-to-move (from-pos to-pos)
"Calculates the total time to move between two positions, assuming
rotation and ascension can occur simultaneously."
(with-accessors ((from-az azimuth) (from-el elevation)) from-pos
(with-accessors ((to-az azimuth) (to-el elevation)) to-pos
(max (time-to-rotate from-az to-az) (time-to-ascend from-el to-el)))))
Lispers are fond of talking about the programmability of the syntax and how easy it is to learn. But the syntax is still there, it’s just encoded positionally rather than with auxiliary words and symbols. For example, the words
azimuth
and
elevation
in the Lisp code denote accessor functions. The outer
with-accessors
macro does something akin to this:
timeToMoveFrom: from_pos to: to_pos
| from_az from_el |
from_az := from_pos azimuth.
from_el := from_pos elevation.
...
So the Lisp is wonderfully terse, but I still feel like I’m tricking something into doing what I want rather than expres
